analysis.one_liner: Adds two years to the patent on the painkiller Ansaid, delaying cheaper generic copies.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved a bill extending the drug Ansaid's patent by 24 months, but it never came to a Senate vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would add 24 months to the patent on Ansaid, a brand-name anti-inflammatory painkiller, as compensation for the years the drug spent waiting for Food and Drug Administration approval [S3]. The bill was tailored so narrowly that it fit essentially one product: a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory whose maker filed its application in 1982, waited at least 78 months, and won approval in 1988 [S2, S4]. A patent gives the maker the exclusive right to sell a drug, so extending it keeps cheaper generic versions off pharmacy shelves for two more years while patients pay brand-name prices.
analysis.who_benefits: The maker of Ansaid, which would get two more years of exclusive sales without generic competition, protected by a formula that extends the patent by the time the application sat at the FDA minus 790 days [S4, S3].

how_it_helps.text: Extends the patent on the drug Ansaid by 24 months beyond its scheduled expiration [S3].
Justifies the extension as repayment for regulatory review time: the patent term grows by the number of days the drug's application was pending at the FDA, minus 790 days [S4].

Applies only to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs whose maker filed a new drug application in 1982, waited at least 78 months for approval, and received approval in 1988 — criteria designed to capture a specific product [S2, S4].

analysis.who_pays: Patients who take the drug and their insurers, who would keep paying brand-name prices for two extra years instead of switching to cheaper generics once the patent expired; generic drug makers also lose the chance to sell copies [S3].

drawbacks.text: Delays generic competition for two years, forcing patients and insurers to continue paying monopoly prices for a drug whose patent would otherwise expire [S3].

The eligibility criteria (filed 1982, waited at least 78 months, approved 1988) are so specific that the bill effectively serves a single product rather than addressing the FDA-review-delay problem across the board [S2, S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The underlying rationale — that a long FDA review eats into a patent's life — is a genuine policy problem, and Congress addressed it generally in other legislation. This bill instead handed a bespoke two-year extension to one drug after the fact, with the entire cost falling on patients through higher prices. The benefit is narrow and private; the cost, though modest in the scheme of federal spending, is real and borne by the public.

outcome.mechanism: The Judiciary Committee approved and reported the bill to the Senate in September 1992, where it sat on the calendar without ever coming up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Introduced by Sen. Levin on May 23, 1991, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee [S6, S1].
The Patents, Copyrights and Trademarks Subcommittee held hearings on August 1, 1991, and approved the bill favorably with a substitute amendment in May 1992 [S6].

The full Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported on August 12, 1992, and reported it favorably on September 22, 1992, with a substitute amendment that converted it into a straight 24-month extension for Ansaid [S6, S3].
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar on September 22, 1992, but was never called up for a floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended [S6, S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and generic drug makers are better off because the bill died: Ansaid's patent monopoly ended on its original schedule instead of running two more years, and cheaper generic versions could reach the market as planned.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote, so no opposition votes exist; its sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor with three cosponsors split 2 Democratic and 1 Republican [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have granted the maker of Ansaid 24 more months of exclusive sales, protected from generic competition [S3]. That extra monopoly time is paid for by patients through continued brand-name prices.

A patent extension keeps generic copies off the market, so generic makers would have been barred from selling lower-priced versions of the drug for two additional years — the same period patients keep paying more.
